problem: Visual semantic navigation (VSN) models are trained and tested almost only in simulators (mostly with RL), so there is no analysis of how they behave on real robots, and no reusable software exists to deploy them.
motivation: Object-goal navigation agents reach near-human performance in Habitat, but it is unknown whether they transfer to real robots. Integrating them requires handling discrete actions, noisy sensors and missing camera actions, which makes real-world testing hard and rare.
key_idea: Release ROS4VSN, a model-agnostic ROS framework that turns discrete VSN actions into real robot motion, and use it to evaluate PIRLNav and VLV on real robots against their simulation results.
insight: Both models lose substantial success rate from sim to real: PIRLNav drops from 65% to 21.11%, VLV from 39% to 29.33%. The gap between them shrinks from 26 to 8 points, and the modular VLV wins in the real world. The authors attribute this to VLV's object detector, which matters most near the target, but they run no ablation to confirm it. The PIRLNav action histogram shows the look-up/look-down substitutions were rarely used, so they are unlikely to explain the drop.
method: discrete_move package: a ROS service executing discrete actions (forward 25 cm, turn 30°, backward, stop) with closed-loop odometry error correction (turn error <0.1°, straight error <5 mm) and trapezoidal acceleration/braking
robot_api and camera_api: hardware abstraction publishing odometry and RGB-D (Orbbec Astra S). Turtlebot 2 uses the standard package, and a custom robot_api was written for LOLA2

visual_semantic_navigation package: collects RGB, depth (temporal median filter) and odometry, queries the VSN model for the next action, requests it from discrete_move, and loops until stop, the step limit or an error

VLV integration: high-level policy stores 12 views (30° turns) per topological node and uses the learned value function plus Mask R-CNN detections to pick a direction. A short-term goal 1.5 m away is reached with a depth-based occupancy map and fast marching low-level planner
PIRLNav integration: RGB plus GPS/compass reconstructed from robot odometry (now noisy). LookUp/LookDown are replaced by backward/forward moves, and a depth-based obstacle check avoids collisions
Real-world protocol: 75 m² apartment, 15 start positions per object category, success if the robot stops within 1 m of the target in <150 actions without collisions

setting.backbone: PIRLNav (CNN+RNN policy, BC + DD-PPO RL fine-tuned, frozen) and VLV (Q-learning value function from YouTube videos + Mask R-CNN + fast-marching planner, frozen)
setting.training_data: No retraining. PIRLNav: 77k human demonstrations on HM3D-Semantics plus RL fine-tuning. VLV: pseudo-labeled real-estate YouTube videos.
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB-D (Orbbec Astra S) plus wheel odometry used as GPS/compass
setting.action_space: Discrete: forward 25 cm, turn left/right 30°, backward 25 cm, stop
setting.simulator: real world only (sim numbers are taken from the original papers in Habitat)

numbers.eval_set_note: 15 start positions per category, 5 categories for VLV (75 episodes)
numbers.extra: no retraining; real robot; <150 actions, no collisions, success within 1 m
numbers.evidence: Table 'Real world success rate against simulation': VLV 29.33% real world, 39% virtual

numbers.eval_set_note: 15 start positions per category, 6 categories for PIRLNav (90 episodes)
numbers.extra: no retraining; real robot; look up/down replaced by backward/forward; GPS/compass from odometry
numbers.evidence: Table 'Real world success rate against simulation': PIRLNav 21.11% real world, 65% virtual

numbers_note: Per-category SRs are in Tables 3 and 4. The 39% and 65% simulation SRs are from the original papers, not this paper's own runs.
results: On a Turtlebot 2, VLV reaches 29.33% SR and PIRLNav 21.11% in the real apartment, versus 39% and 65% in simulation. The modular VLV beats end-to-end PIRLNav in the real world, reversing the simulation ranking. The framework also ran for 5.22 km over 38 hours on two robots without intervention.
limitations: Small-scale evaluation: one 75 m² apartment, 15 episodes per category, and only two models
Explanation for VLV outperforming PIRLNav (object detector) is not tested by ablation
Simulation numbers come from the original papers under different conditions, so the sim-to-real comparison is not strictly controlled
